description.value: This study investigated static and dynamic resting-state functional connectivity within and between intrinsic brain networks in patients with non-complicated mild traumatic brain injury, relating network connectivity to post-traumatic complaints, anxiety, and depression.
Prospective follow-up study of patients with mild traumatic brain injury assessed in the sub-acute phase, with a healthy control group matched for age, sex, education, and handedness.

spans.text: Fifty‐four patients with mTBI (34 with and 20 without complaints) and 20 healthy controls (group‐matched for age, sex, education, and handedness) were included.

value: Static functional connectivity between the bilateral frontal network and salience network was negatively related to HADS-D scores, whereas connectivity between the right frontoparietal network and salience network was positively related to HADS-D scores.

Higher static functional connectivity between the bilateral frontal network and salience network was related to lower HADS-D scores, while higher connectivity between the right frontoparietal network and salience network was related to higher HADS-D scores.

model_representation_notes.value: Dynamic functional connectivity was represented by the standard deviation of sliding-window Fisher Z-transformed correlations across 280 windows.

spans.text: correlations were computed with a sliding‐window approach (window of 20*TR (=40 seconds), steps of 1TR, resulting in a total of 280 windows) and transformed with a Fisher's Z ‐transform. Subsequently, the standard deviation of these 280 correlation values was calculated.

As part of a prospective follow‐up study (UPFRONT study), 54 patients were enrolled in this fMRI study between March 2013 and February 2015 at the University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG), The Netherlands (a level 1 trauma center).

value: Lower functional connectivity of the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus within the left frontoparietal network, and lower connectivity of the medial prefrontal cortex within the bilateral frontal network, were related to higher HADS-A scores.
Higher HADS-A scores in patients with mTBI were associated with weaker functional connectivity within prefrontal and parietal midline areas of the frontoparietal and bilateral frontal network.
